Can a squatter take an Idaho house?

Only by meeting every element of the adverse possession statutes for a full 20 years, which is a hard test in Idaho. A short stay, a few months in a vacant house, or an occupant who moved in with no claim of right is nowhere close.

Idaho has two routes. One covers a person who claims title under a written instrument or a court judgment, and the other covers a person with no paper at all. Both require continuous occupation and possession for 20 years, and the second route adds proof that the land was enclosed or cultivated (Idaho Code 5-207 and 5-210).

For an owner the practical reading is simple. Someone who walks into your house and stays is a problem to solve quickly with the removal tools below, not a title risk that is ticking in any meaningful way.

What a claimant must prove to win by adverse possession

A claimant with no written instrument must show the land was protected by a substantial enclosure or usually cultivated or improved, and must prove it by clear and convincing evidence (Idaho Code 5-210). In no case is adverse possession established unless the land was occupied and claimed continuously for 20 years and the claimant, or the predecessors and grantors, paid all state, county and municipal taxes levied and assessed on it.

The tax element is a major hurdle. An owner who pays the property tax every year and keeps the receipts has a strong answer to a claim. A claimant who never paid the tax cannot meet the statute.

A claimant with a written instrument or judgment has a longer list of ways to show possession. Under Idaho Code 5-208, land counts as possessed in these cases:

  • It has been usually cultivated or improved.
  • It has been protected by a substantial enclosure.
  • Although not enclosed, it has been used for fuel, fencing timber, pasturage or the occupant's ordinary use.
  • A known farm or single lot has been partly improved, and the uncleared part follows the usual custom of the area.

The same clear and convincing standard applies to this route.

Recording a written permission notice

An owner can defeat a boundary or occupancy claim by recording a written instrument with the county recorder stating that the owner did not intend to define boundaries or ownership by permitting the possession. Both 5-208 and 5-210 contain this rule.

It helps most with neighbors and on rural land. If a neighbor's fence, driveway or garden crosses your line, a recorded statement can protect you without a lawsuit and without a fight. Record it in the real estate records of the county where the property sits, and expect the fee schedule in Idaho Code 31-3205 to apply.

If you plan to sell, a clean boundary helps. A buyer's title company will look at fences, shared drives and old agreements, and a recorded permission notice answers a question before anyone asks it.

Which Idaho law fits which kind of unwanted occupant?

The right tool depends on who is in the house and how they got there. Idaho has separate laws for tenants who stay, strangers who enter, and people who remain after being told to leave.

SituationIdaho lawWhat it does
Tenant stays past the lease or fails to payIdaho Code 6-303Unlawful detainer, the civil route to restitution after written notice
Stranger in a residence, owner wants them out nowIdaho Code 6-310AOwner asks the county sheriff for immediate removal on a verified complaint
Person refuses to leave or returns after noticeIdaho Code 18-7008Criminal trespass
Person claims title after many yearsIdaho Code 5-207, 5-208, 5-210Adverse possession, 20 years and tax payment

People who rent or once rented from you fall in a different category. The sheriff process described next does not cover them.

Sheriff removal of squatters

Idaho now lets an owner or the owner's authorized agent ask the county sheriff for immediate removal of people unlawfully occupying a residential dwelling. The law is Idaho Code 6-310A, created by House Bill 321 in 2025.

The owner has to meet every condition:

  • The requester is the owner or the owner's authorized agent.
  • The property includes a residential dwelling.
  • Unauthorized people entered unlawfully and remain or live there.
  • The property was not open to the public when they entered.
  • The owner has directed them to leave.
  • They are not current or former tenants under a written or oral rental agreement the owner authorized.
  • They are not immediate family members of the owner.
  • No litigation over the property is pending between the owner and any known occupant.

The owner submits a completed and verified "Complaint to Remove Persons Unlawfully Occupying Residential Real Property" to the sheriff of the county where the property is located. The sheriff is entitled to the same fee as for serving a writ of restitution. The statute was amended in 2026, so call the sheriff for the current text and the county form before you file.

When the occupant is or was a tenant

A former or current tenant has to be removed through unlawful detainer, not the sheriff shortcut. Under Idaho Code 6-303, a tenant who stays after the term ends without the landlord's permission commits unlawful detainer, and so does one who stays after a default in rent and a three day written notice that demands payment or possession.

The notice must also tell the tenant that, if a court enters judgment, a residential tenant has 72 hours, and a commercial tenant or one with a tract of five acres or more has seven days, to remove belongings before the landlord may dispose of them under section 6-316. Notice for a breach other than rent also runs three days, and the tenant has that time to cure the breach.

An agricultural tenant who holds over more than 60 days after the term ends, with no demand to leave or notice to quit from the landlord, is deemed to hold by permission and may stay another full year. Owners of farm or ranch land should read that rule closely before assuming a holdover can be removed quickly.

Criminal trespass for a house owner

A person commits criminal trespass by entering or remaining on another's real property without permission, knowing or having reason to know that presence is not permitted (Idaho Code 18-7008). Outside a landlord and tenant relationship, a person has reason to know when they fail to leave immediately after the owner or agent tells them to, or when they return without permission within one year.

The statute also finds reason to know on property reasonably associated with a residence or place of business, and on property fenced or enclosed so a reasonable person would see a private boundary. Penalties scale with the facts, with different tiers for first and repeat offenses. A related law, Idaho Code 18-3502, deals with unlawful re-entry of land after a person has been removed by process of law.

Keep your own records: a dated written instruction to leave, photographs, and a log of any return. They make it easier to show what you told the person and when.

Selling a house with an unwanted occupant

A house with a squatter can still be sold, but the occupant usually has to be gone, or the sale terms have to deal with it openly. An unresolved occupant can complicate a conventional sale, since a buyer or title company may ask for vacant possession or a clear lease.

Sellers who need to move faster can start with these steps:

  • Give written notice to leave and keep a copy.
  • Decide which route applies: sheriff removal, unlawful detainer or a trespass report.
  • Pay the property tax and keep receipts, which also defeat an adverse possession claim.
  • Tell any buyer about the occupant in writing.
  • Ask an Idaho attorney before you change locks, move belongings or cut off utilities.

A cash buyer may be willing to take on an occupied property as is, but that is a decision for each buyer and each house, and no result should be assumed in advance.

Frequently asked questions

How long does it take to claim adverse possession in Idaho?

Twenty years of continuous occupation and possession under both the written instrument route and the no instrument route, and the claimant must also have paid all state, county and municipal taxes on the land.

Can I ask the sheriff to remove a squatter in Idaho?

Yes, if you meet every condition in Idaho Code 6-310A: the occupants entered unlawfully, you told them to leave, they are not current or former tenants or immediate family, and no litigation is pending. You file a verified complaint with the sheriff of the county where the home sits.

Is a former tenant a squatter under Idaho law?

No. A tenant who stays after the lease ends or after a rent default and notice is handled through unlawful detainer under Idaho Code 6-303, and the sheriff removal law excludes current and former tenants.

How much notice must a landlord give for unpaid rent in Idaho?

Three days written notice that states the amount due and demands payment or possession, under Idaho Code 6-303(2).

Does paying property tax protect me from a squatter's claim?

It helps a great deal. Idaho Code 5-210 requires a claimant to have paid all taxes levied and assessed on the land, so an owner who pays on time and keeps receipts leaves the claimant unable to satisfy that element.

Landlord tenant law when you sell a rental

Idaho's rental rules are short and mostly sit in two places: the unlawful detainer chapter of Idaho Code title 6 and the tenancy provisions of title 55. They cover deposit refunds, written notices, eviction steps and what a tenant can do when a landlord skips repairs. If you own a house with a tenant in it, the first question is which of those duties follow the property to the buyer.

A sale does not wipe out the tenant's rights. Under Idaho Code 6-321(3), when a rental changes owners during a tenancy, the new owner is liable for refunding the security deposits. The unlawful detainer statute also refers to the landlord's "successor in estate," so the law plainly expects a house to change hands mid-lease.

TopicIdaho CodeRule
Deposit refund6-321(2)Within 21 days if no time is agreed, and in any event within 30 days after the tenant surrenders the premises
Normal wear and tear6-321(1)A landlord may not keep any part of the deposit for it
Nonpayment notice6-303(2)Three days' written notice demanding payment or possession
Tenancy at will55-208Written notice of not less than one month by either side
Tenant moves out after judgment6-316(2)Residential tenant has 72 hours to remove belongings

Security deposits and who owes them after a sale

Money a tenant hands over for any purpose other than rent counts as a security deposit. When the lease ends and the tenant surrenders the unit, the landlord refunds all of it except amounts needed for the contingencies named in the deposit arrangement. Idaho Code 6-321 bars keeping any part of the deposit for normal wear and tear.

Normal wear and tear means deterioration from the use the unit is meant for, without negligence, carelessness, accident, misuse or abuse by the tenant, the household or their guests.

  • Refund within 21 days if the agreement sets no time, and always within 30 days after surrender.
  • If you refund less than the full amount, include a signed statement itemizing what was kept, why, and a detailed list of expenditures from the deposit.
  • If a third-party manager handles the property, the deposit must sit in a separate account at a federally insured institution, apart from the manager's operating account. Owners, certain affiliated managers, real estate licensees and qualifying nonprofits are outside that rule.

Before listing, compare your deposit amounts and lease dates with what the tenant believes they are. The buyer inherits the refund duty, so ask your closing agent how the deposit will be handled and get the answer in writing.

Notices an Idaho landlord can give

Idaho Code 6-303 lists when a tenant becomes guilty of unlawful detainer. That happens if they stay after the lease term ends without permission, after a rent default and a three day written notice, or after breaking another lease condition and a three day notice.

The rent notice must demand the stated amount due or possession of the property. It must also warn that if a court enters judgment, a residential tenant will have 72 hours to remove belongings. It may be served at any time within one year after the rent becomes due.

  • Nonpayment. Three days' written notice demanding the stated rent or possession.
  • Other lease violations. Three days' written notice requiring performance or possession. Within those three days, the tenant or an interested person can cure the problem or pay and save the lease from forfeiture, unless the violation cannot be performed afterward.
  • Assigning, subletting or waste. A tenant who does this contrary to the lease ends the lease, and the landlord can serve a three day notice to quit.
  • Controlled substances. Unlawful delivery, production or use on the leased premises during the term is also a ground under the statute.

A tenant on farmland who holds over more than 60 days after the term with no demand or notice to quit is deemed to hold by permission for another full year.

Ending a month to month tenancy before a sale

A tenancy at will, however it began, ends when either side gives written notice of not less than one month. Under Idaho Code 55-208 the landlord's written notice must tell the tenant to leave within a period of at least one month, stated in the notice. The tenant ends it by written notice naming the date they will vacate, also at least one month out.

The unlawful detainer statute ties into this. For a tenancy at will, the landlord has to end it by notice first, as the civil code prescribes, before the tenant counts as holding over unlawfully.

If you want the house empty at closing, send the written notice early and keep a copy. Plan on at least a month from the notice date before a tenant at will can be required to go.

How an eviction ends and what tenants can remove

Once a court rules for the landlord, the tenant has a short window to take belongings, and then the sheriff restores possession. Under Idaho Code 6-316(2), a residential tenant has 72 hours to remove belongings. A commercial tenant, or a tenant with a tract of five acres or more, has seven days, and a court may give a commercial tenant longer for good cause.

The landlord or the landlord's agent may deliver a writ of restitution, or hand the sheriff a copy and ask the sheriff to deliver it. After the removal period, and three days after the court's finding, the sheriff restores possession by removing the tenant. The landlord may then remove and dispose of remaining property, subject to any security interests, without further compensation to the tenant.

The court can also award the landlord reasonable costs for removing property and restoring the premises when good cause is shown. Eviction is a court process with fixed steps, and the statute sends removal through the sheriff, so a seller cannot shortcut it.

When the landlord does not make repairs

A tenant can sue for damages and specific performance, but first has to give three days' written notice listing each failure. Idaho Code 6-320 allows the action for failure to provide reasonable waterproofing and weather protection, failure to maintain landlord-supplied electrical, plumbing, heating, ventilating, cooling or sanitary facilities, hazardous conditions, failure to return a deposit when required, breach of a lease term materially affecting health and safety, and failure to install approved smoke detectors.

If the landlord does not perform or cure within three days after service, the tenant may file. In an action solely for specific performance, the court must set trial within 12 days of the complaint, and service must come at least five days before trial. A claim that also seeks damages does not get that fast schedule.

Smoke detectors have their own process. The landlord must verify at the start of the rental that working detectors are installed. If not, the tenant can send written notice by certified mail, and if detectors are not installed within 72 hours of receipt, the tenant may install them and deduct the cost from the next month's rent. The section does not apply to tracts of five acres or more used for agricultural purposes.

If you plan to sell a tenant-occupied house, fix or document any open repair items first.

Steps before selling a house with tenants

Gather the lease and deposit records first, then decide whether the tenant stays or leaves.

  1. Locate the signed lease, any addenda, and proof of the deposit amount and where it is held.
  2. Check whether rent is current and whether any notice has already been served.
  3. Decide whether the tenant will stay under the existing lease or whether you will give written notice for a tenancy at will.
  4. Tell the closing agent how the deposit will transfer to the buyer.

Our Idaho squatters rights and adverse possession guide covers people who stay without a lease. For lease questions, the Idaho Court Assistance Office offers self-help information at courtselfhelp.idaho.gov.

Selling for cash with a tenant in place

We can buy a house with tenants in it, as it stands. We review the lease, the deposit and the condition of the property before making any offer, and we do not quote a price here. The existing tenancy goes with the sale, so the deposit refund duty passes to the new owner under 6-321(3).

A cash purchase does not skip the legal steps for ending a tenancy. If you want the tenant out, the notices and court steps above still apply. This page is general information, not legal advice, so confirm details with the court, the county sheriff or an Idaho attorney.

Frequently asked questions

How long does an Idaho landlord have to return a security deposit?

Within 21 days if the agreement fixes no time, and in any event within 30 days after the tenant surrenders the premises. A partial refund needs a signed itemized statement.

Who owes the tenant's deposit when a rental house is sold?

The new owner. Idaho Code 6-321(3) says that if the property changes ownership during a tenancy, the new owner is liable for refund of the deposits.

How much notice must a landlord give for unpaid rent?

Three days' written notice stating the amount due and demanding payment or possession. The notice must also warn that a residential tenant has 72 hours after a judgment to remove belongings.

How much notice ends a month to month tenancy?

At least one month in writing, from either the landlord or the tenant, under Idaho Code 55-208. The notice must specify the date.

Can I sell a house that has tenants?

Yes. The sale does not end the tenancy, and the new owner takes over the deposit refund duty. A cash buyer can purchase a rented house as it stands, after reviewing the lease and condition.
